chapter: Big band, Chicago players, recordings and gospel
title: Milt Jackson's New York rhythm section and Wilbur Campbell
summary: DeMichael describes Milt Jackson dissatisfied with his bass and drums in Chicago and wishing for Wilbur Campbell; Saunders ties this to the Modern Jazz Quartet's unity.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: I was talking to Milt Jackson last week, went down to hear him a couple of times. I was so -- and so was he and everybody else -- Teddy Edwards, --
-- with the bass player and drummer, and particularly the drummer. I never saw Bags really turn around to somebody on the stand and tell him how to play, but he did then.
And when I was leaving, I said, I'll
be back next week. He says, ah, Wilbur Campbell. I said, that's right.
Well, that's good, right, right. But, see, he's from that school of unity.
He worked all of those years with the Jazz Quartet.
And they were just like a glove on your hand. And so that's -- when you break into something like that, then other things kind of disturb you if you don't get it, yeah.
Right, but, he knew that there are better musicians available in Chicago that these guys from New York.
And it was unfortunate, because Barry Harris and Teddy Edwards and Bags --
But the rhythm section not very, but the bass player and drummer. Just drive me crazy.
and -- oh, I mean, it was really amateurville.
I told them, I said, I'll be back next week.
